The Texas Instruments TMX 1795: the first, forgotten microprocessor

Equally impressive are some of the processors from the next generation, notably the Zilog Z80, MOS 6502, and others. I still remember working with the Apple II which, if I recall, ran a 6502 clocked at around 1MHz. Years later, we worked with the BBC micro which also ran a 6502A at a faster clock speed. What was amazing about the BBC micro (the beeb) was the power you could unleash through direct inline assembly, it was truly a learner's machine.

The Z80 was truly a pioneer in many ways. It was among the first processors at that price point that had built in block shift instructions, something that was rare in much more powerful & expensive processors of the day. The CPIR/CPDR instructions gave you the ability to automatically search for a value in a chunk of memory! LDIR/LDDR gave you memory copy without looping. INIR/OTIR gave you high speed IO to peripherals with just four instructions.

You still see these processors today in embedded systems, consumer electronics, PLC's, robots, and so on. Many smart cards still run an 8051 core.

I guess I'm getting old, but it is wonderful to see how the bleeding edge stuff from my day is still being put to great use.
